name: Archetype: linear warfare armies (1600-1789)

weightNotes.aggression: Trained long-service soldiers were expensive and hard to replace, which was 'a major deterrent to battle' (warhistory.org, Prussian practice 1740-1763); generals often manoeuvred for months without fighting. Frederick II was the aggressive exception.
weightNotes.maneuver: Lines advanced very slowly, giving the enemy time to shift reserves; armies manoeuvred against each other's supply lines rather than seeking destruction (warhistory.org).
weightNotes.flanking: Cavalry on the wings tried to outflank the enemy; Frederick's oblique order (Leuthen 1757) refused one wing and attacked the other in echelon (warhistory.org). Most battles were still parallel-line firefights.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Fortress warfare dominated (Vauban's sieges, the Low Countries campaigns of the Spanish and Austrian Succession wars); campaigns were often decided by which fortresses fell. High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Standard order of battle was two lines about 200 m apart, the second acting as reserve to relieve the first or stop a cavalry breakthrough (warhistory.org). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Hussars and light troops screened and patrolled, mainly as security against desertion and raids (Frederick, General Principles of War); operational reconnaissance was patchy.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.gunpowder mid 0.26, grade C. The gunpowder baseline (CDB90 1600-1788) is drawn from linear-warfare armies, so the archetype sits on it.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Infantry in the centre, cavalry on the wings, battalion guns between battalions: three arms on one field, but in rigid separate roles with little mutual support (warhistory.org).
weightNotes.initiative: Rigid drill and close supervision, partly to prevent desertion of soldiers 'tied to no bond' with the state (Frederick, General Principles of War). Very low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies lived from magazines (Louvois' system, about 15 days' reserve; Jelinek, DTIC AD1022125) and stayed within a few marches of them; Frederick judged wars far from one's borders 'useless'. High.

summary: Standing professional armies of long-service soldiers, many of them foreign or pressed, fought in long thin lines three ranks deep, infantry in the centre and cavalry on the wings, trading volleys at close range. Drill gave fire discipline and kept men from deserting. Armies moved slowly, tied to magazines and bread ovens, and much of every war was fortress warfare: Vauban-style sieges and entrenched lines. Battles were costly and rarely decisive because beaten armies usually withdrew intact and pursuit was weak.
whyItWorked: Disciplined volley fire made the line the most effective way to use smoothbore muskets, and the magazine system let armies campaign without destroying the country they depended on. Limited war suited dynastic states with limited money and men. In the right hands (Frederick at Rossbach and Leuthen, 1757) the system could still deliver decisive victories.
whereItFailed: Battles were attritional and rarely ended wars (Malplaquet 1709, Zorndorf 1758, Kunersdorf 1759); pursuit was weak. Line troops fighting irregulars in broken terrain were cut up (Braddock at the Monongahela, 1755). Against mass conscript armies living off the land and fighting in columns and skirmish swarms, the system collapsed (Valmy and Jemappes 1792, Jena 1806).
